title: Streamline inflight-session pruning and scheduler backpressure pathways
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Summary: Reduce complexity and tail-latency by refactoring the continuous-batcher session lifecycle and simplifying scheduler backpressure logic. We want to remove multiple locking hotpaths, consolidate session pruning into a single async GC pathway, and replace the current hysteresis-based backpressure with a stabilized, thresholded admission controller.

Background: Over the last two years the batcher and KV cache subsystems accumulated incremental fixes to keep latency SLOs stable under varied load. Those changes layered lease migration, dual-path pruning, and admission heuristics that are hard to reason about and make future optimizations risky. This ticket scopes a cohesive refactor to address that tech debt while keeping runtime correctness and graceful degradation targets.

Goals:
- Simplify inflight session lifecycle state machine (remove 'migrate' and 'quiesce' transient states).
- Move pruning/eviction of session metadata off the scheduler hotpath into an async GC worker with bounded CPU.
- Replace per-slot spinlocks with lock-free readpath where safe; use fine-grained mutexes for rare writes.
- Unify backpressure signals to two metrics (inflight_count and queue_depth) and a time-smoothed threshold.
- Upgrade Tokio runtime from 1.23 -> 1.28 to pick up scheduling and timer improvements; pin to 1.28.1.

Success criteria / acceptance tests:
- P99 generation latency for 1k token requests under representative mix reduced by >= 5% vs baseline.
- Scheduler CPU usage reduced by >= 15% at 95th percentile under synthetic multi-tenant load.
- KV eviction churn (evict/reinsert cycles) reduced by >= 30% on long-lived streams.
- No customer-facing errors introduced during rolling canary deploys; < 0.1% increase in 5xx during rollout is allowed.
- Unit and integration test coverage for the new session state transitions + fuzzed migration scenarios.

Design artifacts: Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/streamline-inflight-session-pruning
Prototype benchmark: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/bench/streamline-prune-2026
PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4567

Planned approach:
1) Implement a small adapter that routes pruning requests to an async GC worker (configurable concurrency).
2) Introduce epoch-based tombstone markers for sessions to avoid lengthy lease migrations; tombstones allow safe late readers for a bounded window.
3) Rework admission controller: compute smoothed inflight_count over 250ms window and compare to configurable thresholds per slot; when over threshold reject with fast-fail that returns structured retry-after.
4) Remove stale migration code paths and add feature flags to toggle behavior during rollout.
5) Run cluster-scale A/B perf tests and iterate.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Tombstone window misconfiguration could cause early eviction affecting long-running streams. Mitigation: conservative default windows, rollouts behind feature flag, canary on non-critical regions.
- Risk: Tokio upgrade surface-change. Mitigation: upgrade in isolated dependency bump commit, run full integration matrix in CI.
- Risk: Undetected regressions in adversarial hotkey workloads. Mitigation: add targeted hotkey simulation to perf suite and run blackhole tests before canary.

Rollout plan:
- Merge behind feature flag, deploy to internal staging, run 48h soak with traffic generator.
- Canary 2% traffic in us-west for 24h -> 10% for 12h -> 50% for 8h -> full. Abort thresholds: >0.2% increase in request errors, or >10% regression in P99 latency.

Owner: Marco Li (runtime infra). Reviewers: Priya Patel, Ryan O'Connor, Lina Morales.

2026-03-01 - Ryan O'Connor: Code review notes - prefer atomic swaps for the session state pointer to reduce ABA risks. Also flagged that the current log lines are too chatty on hot paths; recommend sampling logs and adding structured metrics instead.
